    People also ask
    What is a filibuster in simple terms?
    An AI Overview is not available for this searchCan't generate an AI overview right now. Try again later.
    AI Overview
    A filibuster is a
    U.S. Senate tactic used by minority senators to delay or block a vote on a bill by prolonging debate indefinitely. Because Senate rules allow unlimited debate, a bill often requires a 60-vote majority (known as cloture) to end the stalling tactic, rather than a simple 51-vote majority to pass. 
    Key Aspects of a Filibuster: 
    • Purpose: To stop a bill the minority party opposes from passing, or to force changes to it.
    • How it Works: In the past, this involved long speeches (talking a bill to death). Today, it is often just a public threat to filibuster, which forces the Senate to either find 60 votes to break it or move on to other business
      .
    • Breaking a Filibuster (Cloture): To stop the filibuster, a "cloture motion" must be filed and voted on. This requires 60 votes to succeed.
    • Result: If the minority can maintain 41 or more votes against the cloture, they can kill the legislation. 
    While not in the U.S. Constitution, the filibuster has become a staple of Senate procedures.
